newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO to push on with enlargement next year.
newsitem.headline: NATO to push on with enlargement next year.

text.p: NATO countries said on Thursday they would press ahead with expansion plans next year and grant full membership to former communist enemies in eastern and central Europe despite Russian objections.

"At a summit next year several countries will be invited to start accession talks," U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters after a two-day informal meeting of the 16-nation alliance's defence ministers in Bergen, Norway.
Perry declined to be drawn on which countries may be invited to join the alliance, but emphasised the process would go ahead whatever Moscow's concerns.
"If I thought that those actions (expansion) were threatening Russia I would have a very different view, but I don't believe that for a minute," Perry said.

Since the end of the Cold War, ex-Communist countries have been seeking to join NATO to guarantee their future security against Russia. Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are the most likely candidates, but could be joined by Slovenia.

NATO hopes to buy off Russia by offering it a new all- embracing security pact in the form of a treaty or charter which it says it will negotiate in parallel with its first enlargement since the late 1970s.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who met the ministers for a separate "16+1" session after the main session, repeated Moscow's view that it considered there was "no strategic necessity" to enlarge the alliance.
"Our country does not want the NATO expansion at present... we in our country are concerned," he told a press conference.

But Rodionov notably steered clear of the fiery rhethoric that accompanied a virulent anti-enlargement campaign by Moscow last year and said his country was ready to work with NATO on the planning of a possible new peace force for Bosnia.
"We are ready to cooperate," he told reporters.

Maintaining Russian public opinion was firmly opposed to any alliance expansion, Rodionov hinted Moscow's position could change as growing cooperation with NATO changed public perception of its Cold War foe.
"We may support this idea when our public is convinced that NATO has indeed passed through a genuine transformation in accordance with the new conditions of the political situation."
Rodionov also said the dispute over enlargement should not stand in the way of cooperation in other areas, such as Bosnia.
"That (Bosnia) is another matter, one thing is not in contradiction with another," he said in reply to a question.

NATO is hoping it can entice Russia to take part actively in the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme designed to try and fill a security vacuum in central and eastern Europe created by the collapse of communism.
The alliance wants to upgrade PFP and offer it as an alternative to countries left out of next year's expansion, but which still want an insurance policy against a rebirth of an expansionist Russia.

"What we are doing with NATO and what we are doing with Partnership for Peace is creating a security circle for all of Europe... our goal is not to threaten Russia, but to bring Russia into that security circle," Perry said.

NATO diplomats say the aim is to try to dovetail approval of both enlargement and a new pact for Russia at next year's heads of government summit which would also endorse reform of the alliance's command structures.
